title: How do you Deal with Future Copyright Protection for Generated Asset
author: Zealousideal_Feed_41
selftext:
So far I am done with generated audios/sound for the app I am planning to make, on this current stage I have learn about the copyright issues I might face if I am not careful with generating asset.

Let's say I used a copyrighted image as a reference and I changed it completely I am still possible to face a copyright strike in the future? if i need to show the proof of prompt they will see that it came from a copyrighted reference.

Even so you are safe from copyright the rules is you cannot claim a copyright for an ai image asset. Others can copy your creation and you cannot do anythung about it because it is treated as public domain.

I am in delima I am thinking for the what could happen in the future and at the same time I am looking for answer how to deal with this. How do you guys go around with this?

comments.author: Novaworld7
comments.body: Ask\* a lawyer legal questions. Reddit is not a general counsel nor should you take anyone on here at their word.

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
It's good that you're thinking about this, but the unfortunate answer is "by and large nobody knows."  Much of this is completely untested in a courtroom, and it's generally up to the copyright holder to enforce infringement.

If you used a copyrighted image as a reference and changed it *completely,* it depends on how you did it.  If you fed it into an img2img workflow and used the output, it *could* be argued that you infringed copyright because that's not fair use - your intention was to distribute and monetize the output.  But it could also be argued that the resulting work is completely derivative so you're not distributing anything copyrighted, and *inference* for an AI model has been regularly ruled to not be infringement.  And also it's completely impossible to prove that any of that happened (again, if it's truly "completely different") so the enforcement angle falls apart either way.

>Even so you are safe from copyright the rules is you cannot claim a copyright for an ai image asset. Others can copy your creation and you cannot do anythung about it because it is treated as public domain.

This is also "we don't know."  There was one single ruling that wholly generative AI content cannot be copyrighted in the US.  That establishes a single datapoint of precedent, but doesn't magically solve the whole legal issue like people on reddit claim.  And again, it falls to how much of what you do with that output is *derivative* of that output.  If you edit it, at some nebulous point it *does* become copyrightable again, as that case only ruled about pure, untouched AI output without "substantial human contribution." What does that mean?  Nobody knows until it finds a courtroom and establishes broader case law.

Honestly unless you're wholesale ripping off copyrighted assets and barely changing them, this isn't the meaningful legal worry. What *is* the meaningful legal worry is *provenance*.  Do you actually have ownership and commercial distribution rights under the licensing model of whatever AI tool you used to generate the content?  Free tiers of services generally do not, paid tiers *usually* do, and all of it still falls under "can anybody prove that you got this from there and which license you had."  Which is why output watermarking is such a hot topic at the moment.  But it's still up to them to come after you - If you generated something with a fine-tune of Illustrious locally on your machine that doesn't have a commercial distribution license, is the person who made that fine-tune going to tear apart your game to try to prove where that single image came from?  Can they even tell?  If they can tell, can they **prove it**? Does their license even have any legal weight given they likely built that model on things *they themselves* had no license for?

It's a legal clusterfuck top to bottom.

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body:
>Let's say I used a copyrighted image as a reference and I changed it completely I am still possible to face a copyright strike in the future

People have been doing that for *decades*. Hell, in the 90s they would trace over sprites from more popular games and just change the outfits. Even today they'll design characters using pictures of real people and change enough so that it's not an exact likeness.

Either way, question for a lawyer, with examples, not for reddit.

comments.author: tipsystatistic
comments.body:
As the laws stand today:

-Changing copyrighted work (even completely) is creating derivative work. Unless you have permission, that’s infringement.

-Purely AI generated content can’t be copyrighted.
If it wasn’t substantially modified by a human, anyone can re-use it and you can’t claim infringement.

-If AI writes every line of code and generates all the assets, it may be public domain. This comes down to specifics but there’s a non zero chance that you have no copyright claim to a game you spent thousands of hours testing and directing.

comments.author: MessageSelfdestructs
comments.body:
Sorry, but how would people know an image of yours is generated: **definitely** if you then also manually manipulated it afterwards?

If you don't leave any obvious tells in the image... I'm not too sure how people would know.

Also, if the image is part of your app, I don't see why you would even need to copyright it... Unless it's your logo, but other than that I can't see many images in an app that would require to be copyrighted. And a logo can easily be recreated by yourself to completely dodge an accusation of it being AI generated.

But as others advised: if you truly want legal advice, you should ask an actual lawyer. Not Reddit.

Your game as a whole is still protected, individual pieces that are AI generated is not, though if people want to steal your assets would have stolen them regardless and even if you have copyright it's not necessarily financially viable to go after them.
